subtitle: The order in the middle of the sentence, and dass or zu
words.intro: Millions of Germans leave their town to go to work. So every morning at 6:42 the same people get on the same carriage, sit in the same seats, and never speak.

grammar[0].fact: Nothing in the middle of a German sentence is strictly wrong: the order signals what you think is new. The last place gets the weight. So *Ich fahre morgen nach Rom* and *Ich fahre nach Rom morgen* are both possible, and the second one means someone just asked you *when*.

grammar[1].fact: Your regular seat is your *Stammplatz*, and Germans take these seriously: at a *Stammtisch* the sign on the table in the pub says who sits there, and it may have said so for decades. Sit there and someone will come over and politely explain.

document.intro: A real Deutschlandticket on a smart card, with the name blanked out. The small print is the voice of every contract. *Nicht übertragbar* means you can’t pass it on. *Es gelten die …* means the following rules apply.
document.fact: At first the ticket cost 49 euros a month, and the price has gone up since. It’s valid on all local trains, buses and trams in the country, but not on the fast trains. Hamburg to Munich is possible, if you have most of a day.
document.tasks[1].instruction: Join the sentences, with zu if the person is the same.

document.tasks[1].items[2].answer: Ich versuche, mit ihm zu sprechen.
reading.intro: Lena now commutes to a job in Hanover. For eleven months she has sat opposite the same man in seat 54, at 6:42. They have never exchanged a word. Today, she decides to talk to him. She has been practising for a week, and she has a sentence ready.
reading.fact: German long-distance trains have a quiet zone, the *Ruhebereich*, and passengers will enforce it. Since 2023 the *Deutschlandticket* has given commuters one flat monthly price for all local transport in the country.
